newsitem.title: GERMANY: German builders facing continued slump-studies.
newsitem.headline: German builders facing continued slump-studies.

text.p: Two new studies on the German construction sector, the country's largest industry, made clear on Friday that Germany's builders must reckon with a further two years of declining construction spending.
The studies came amid renewed pressure on the industry, already in the middle of sharp price competition, to reduce yet further its costs, seen as among the highest in the world.

Presenting a new study at a construction industry conference in Leipzig, the Ifo research institute said total construction investment in Germany fell 2.5 percent in 1996 and predicted a further fall of one percent this year.
It put total German construction spending at 410.0 billion marks ($238.1 billion) in 1996, dropping to 406.9 billion this year and 405.9 billion the year after.
Earlier, the Association of the German Construction Industry said it expected building investment this year to fall 2.2 percent in real terms.

German construction minister Klaus Toepfer told the Leipzig conference the post-unification building boom that had fizzled out two years ago had meant that the sector in the meantime had failed to make the structural changes it needed to remain competitive.
He said the deep unemployment among builders, currently at some 400,000 compared to the 1.3 million actually in work, had become "a social and political problem of the highest order".

Toepfer urged German construction firms to commit themselves to the new technology that many of their international rivals had successfully embraced over the last few years to become more competitive.

He further hoped that wage negototions due to start shortly in the sector would lead to "sensible" solutions and said the recently proposed deal providing employees with continued salaries in times of bad weather was "a step in the right direction" by reducing joblessness.

Toepfer also said a recently-announced government programme offering cheap loan facilities on up to 25 billion marks of funds targeting building projects had met with "significant demand", without giving further details.

Highlighting one of the industry's main problems, a German state finance minister involved in one of the country's most ambitious rebuilding projects told the conference construction was being hampered by prohibitively high costs.
Georg Milbradt, finance minister for the state of Saxony, said new building and financing methods were required to make construction affordable.
"Construction is simply too expensive...It cannot go on like this," said Milbradt, who has a role in funding the billion-mark redevelopment of the former Communist-controlled eastern state of Saxony.
He said Germany stood far behind the United States and Japan in the degree of automisation involved in the construction process, while too little risk was being taken on the financing of projects.
East German firms were moreover still unable to afford minimum wages across the industry set out by new laws, he said.

Milbradt's comments follow the decision of the Transrapid high-speed rail consortium last month to part company with German building firms originally due to build the infrastructure and open the project out to open tender in a bid to dave building costs. ($ = 1.722 German Marks)
